lessons.title: Classes, Records and Enums
lessons.explanation:
# 05 · Classes, Records and Enums

Up to now the exercises were static methods: data in, answer out. Real
projects are made of *types* — a `Book`, a `BankAccount`, an `Order`, a
`Priority` — that own their data and refuse to be put in an invalid
state. This module is about designing those types so that bugs become
impossible rather than merely unlikely.

From here on the thing you edit is often a nested type above the tests.
The prompt always says which one.

## The mental model

### 1 · A record is a named tuple with free equality

```java
record Book(String isbn, String title, int year) {
    Book {                                   // compact constructor
        if (title == null || title.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("title");
        title = title.strip();               // reassign the PARAMETER
    }
}
```

Records give you the constructor, private final fields, accessors
(`title()`), `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`. Use them for values:
things identified by their contents.

### 2 · A class owns state and guards it

```java
final class BankAccount {
    private long balanceCents;               // nobody else can write this
    void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(...);   // bad argument
        if (cents > balanceCents) throw new IllegalStateException(...); // bad timing
        balanceCents -= cents;               // check first, change last
    }
}
```

### 3 · Enums are classes with a fixed set of instances

```java
enum Priority {
    LOW("L", 7), HIGH("H", 1);
    private final String code; private final int daysToDue;
    Priority(String code, int days) { this.code = code; this.daysToDue = days; }
}
```

Per-constant data goes next to the constant. `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` are
the fast, ordered collections for enum keys.

### 4 · Interfaces name a capability; sealed interfaces close the family

```java
interface Discount { long apply(long cents); }
record PercentOff(int percent) implements Discount { ... }

sealed interface Command permits Add, Complete, Rename {}
```

## The details that bite

1. **Override `equals` and you must override `hashCode`**, from the same
   fields — or `HashSet`/`HashMap` silently break.
2. **`equals(Isbn other)` is an overload, not an override.** The
   parameter must be `Object`. Put `@Override` on it.
3. **`final` stops reassignment, not mutation.** A `final List` can still
   be added to. Copy in (`List.copyOf`) and don't leak mutable state out.
4. **`valueOf("m")` matches constant NAMES**, case-sensitively. Look up
   your own codes with a loop or a map.
5. **Never persist `ordinal()`.** Reordering constants changes it.
6. **`IllegalArgumentException` = the caller passed garbage;
   `IllegalStateException` = the object can't do that right now.**
7. **Validate in the constructor**, and every instance is valid — no
   `isValid()` to forget.
8. **Java 17 has `instanceof` patterns, not pattern `switch`** (that is
   Java 21). Dispatch on a sealed family with an if-chain.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-record-book.java` | ★☆☆ | a Book record that validates and trims itself |
| 02 | `02-bank-account.java` | ★☆☆ | an encapsulated account: deposit, withdraw, no overdraft |
| 03 | `03-equals-and-hashcode.java` | ★★☆ | an Isbn value class that works in sets and maps |
| 04 | `04-priority-enum.java` | ★★☆ | an enum with codes, raise(), and an EnumMap count |
| 05 | `05-discount-interface.java` | ★★☆ | three discount strategies behind one interface |
| 06 | `06-question-builder.java` | ★★☆ | a fluent builder that validates at build() |
| 07 | `07-sealed-commands.java` | ★★★ | to-do commands as a sealed family of records |
| 08 | `08-immutable-order.java` | ★★★ | an Order with no way in or out for mutation |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/06-exceptions-and-files`

unit.title: An order nobody can tamper with

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/01.instructions:
**Concepts:** records · compact constructors · validation · withers  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A library tracker's Book is a record. Finish it (the nested record
Book, above the tests): its compact constructor trims the title and
refuses, with IllegalArgumentException, a null or blank isbn or title
and a year outside 1450..2100. withTitle returns a COPY with a new
title — validated like any other book.

    new Book("9780441172719", " Dune ", 1965).title()  → "Dune"
    new Book("9780441172719", "  ", 1965)    → IllegalArgumentException
    dune.withTitle("Dune Messiah")           → a new Book; dune unchanged

hint: in a compact constructor you assign the PARAMETER, not this.title.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/01.explanation:
A record declares its data once — `record Book(String isbn, String
title, int year)` — and gets the constructor, private final fields,
accessors (title(), not getTitle()), equals, hashCode and toString for
free. What it does NOT get for free is validity; that is the compact
constructor's job.
The compact form `Book { ... }` has no parameter list: it runs BEFORE
the fields are assigned, with the parameters in scope, and the fields
are assigned from the parameters automatically at the end. So to
normalise you reassign the parameter — `title = title.strip();` — and
the field gets the cleaned value. Writing this.title = ... is a
compile error there.
Validate in the constructor and the invariant holds for EVERY Book in
the program, including ones built by withTitle, deserialisers and
tests. That is the payoff: no "isValid()" method to forget to call.
Records are immutable (shallowly), so "changing" one means building a
new one: a wither, withTitle, calls the canonical constructor, and so
is validated for free.
Note the check order: null and blank before strip(), or strip() throws
NullPointerException with a useless message.

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/02.instructions:
**Concepts:** encapsulation · private fields · guard clauses · exceptions  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

The bank simulator's first class. Finish the nested class BankAccount:
the owner name is required (IllegalArgumentException when blank); a new
account starts at 0; deposit and withdraw take positive cent amounts
(anything else → IllegalArgumentException); withdrawing more than the
balance → IllegalStateException and the balance is unchanged.

    var acct = new BankAccount("Ada");
    acct.deposit(5_000);  acct.withdraw(1_250);   acct.balance() → 3750
    acct.withdraw(10_000)                          → IllegalStateException

hint: check everything first, change state last.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/02.explanation:
Encapsulation is not "add getters". It is: the object owns its state,
and the ONLY way to change it is through methods that keep it valid.
A public balance field (or a setBalance) lets any caller write -1; a
private field with deposit/withdraw makes negative balances impossible
by construction.
Two kinds of "no": a non-positive amount is the CALLER's bug — a bad
argument — so IllegalArgumentException. Withdrawing more than you have
is a perfectly well-formed request that the current STATE can't honour
— IllegalStateException. Picking the right one tells the caller whether
to fix their code or to handle a business outcome.
Order inside each method: validate everything, THEN mutate. If you
subtract first and check after, a failed withdraw has already damaged
the balance by the time it throws. "Check, then act" keeps a failed
call side-effect free, which the last test checks.
Cents as long: integer arithmetic, no rounding, and long gives room
for big balances. Module 07 moves to BigDecimal for rates and interest.

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/03.instructions:
**Concepts:** equals · hashCode · HashSet/HashMap contracts · normalisation  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

ISBNs arrive as "978-0-441-17271-9", "978 0441172719" or plain digits.
Finish the nested class Isbn: the constructor keeps only the digits
(fewer or more than 13 → IllegalArgumentException); two Isbns are equal
when their digits are; equal Isbns must hash alike, so sets and maps
treat them as one key; toString is the 13 digits.

    new Isbn("978-0-441-17271-9").equals(new Isbn("9780441172719"))
                                    → true
    both added to one HashSet       → size 1
    new Isbn("978-0")               → IllegalArgumentException

hint: override BOTH equals(Object) and hashCode, from the same field.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/03.explanation:
HashSet and HashMap find things in two steps: hashCode picks a bucket,
then equals compares within it. The contract: equal objects MUST have
equal hash codes. Override only equals and two equal Isbns land in
different buckets — contains says false, the set holds "duplicates",
and map.get with an equal key returns null. Every test here that uses
a set or map catches that.
Normalise once, in the constructor, and base both methods on the
normalised field. Then equality is cheap and unambiguous: digits.equals
(other.digits), and hashCode is digits.hashCode().
equals(Object) has a fixed shape: same reference → true; not an Isbn
(including null) → false; then compare fields. `o instanceof Isbn
other` does the type check, the null check and the cast in one step.
The parameter type must be Object: writing equals(Isbn other) is an
OVERLOAD, not an override — collections never call it. @Override on
both methods turns that mistake into a compile error.
Why not a record? A record Isbn(String digits) would get equals and
hashCode free, but the compact constructor can only reassign the
parameter — which works too. A class is used here so you write the
contract by hand once.

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/04.instructions:
**Concepts:** enum fields · values() · EnumMap · ordinal order  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A to-do manager's Priority enum carries a one-letter code and how many
days a task of that priority may wait. Finish its methods (the enum is
above the tests; its constructor is done): fromCode looks a code up
case-insensitively (unknown → IllegalArgumentException); raise returns
the next more urgent priority (HIGH stays HIGH); countAll counts a list
of priorities into a map that has EVERY priority as a key, in enum
order.

    Priority.fromCode("m")              → MEDIUM
    Priority.LOW.raise()                → MEDIUM
    countAll(List.of(HIGH, HIGH))       → {LOW=0, MEDIUM=0, HIGH=2}

hint: values() returns the constants in declaration order.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/04.explanation:
An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances, so it can have
fields, a constructor and methods. Data that belongs to each constant
(code, daysToDue) goes in the constructor call next to the constant,
not in a switch somewhere else — adding a URGENT constant then forces
you to supply its data right there.
fromCode loops over values() and compares with equalsIgnoreCase. A
switch or a static Map<String, Priority> built once in a static block
would also do; for three constants the loop is clearest. Do NOT use
valueOf(code) here — valueOf matches the constant NAME ("MEDIUM"), and
throws for "m".
raise uses declaration order: values()[ordinal() + 1], clamped at the
last one. ordinal() is fine INSIDE the enum, where the order is
defined; outside, never persist or compute with ordinals — reordering
the constants silently changes every stored number.
countAll wants an EnumMap: a map specialised for enum keys, backed by
an array, iterating in declaration order. Pre-filling every key with 0
means callers never meet a null for "no tasks of that priority".

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/05.instructions:
**Concepts:** interfaces · records implementing interfaces · polymorphism  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An order system supports several discount kinds behind one interface,
Discount (above the tests), whose apply(cents) returns the new price.
Finish the three records: NoDiscount; PercentOff(percent) takes that
percent off, the discount rounded to the nearest cent, halves up;
AmountOff(cents) takes a fixed amount off but never goes below zero.
Then write best: the discount giving the lowest price (the first one
wins a tie; an empty list means no discount).

    new PercentOff(15).apply(999)    → 849     (149.85 rounds to 150)
    new AmountOff(500).apply(300)    → 0
    best(List.of(pct10, off300), 2000).apply(2000)   → 1700

hint: a half-up integer rounding of a / 100 is (a + 50) / 100 for a ≥ 0.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/05.explanation:
An interface names a capability — "can turn a price into a discounted
price" — and lets unrelated types provide it. The caller holds a
Discount and calls apply; WHICH apply runs is decided at runtime by the
object's class. That is polymorphism, and it is what lets best() treat
every discount kind identically and lets you add a BuyOneGetOne next
month without touching best().
Records can implement interfaces, which makes small strategy objects
like these one-liners with free equals and toString.
PercentOff stays in integer cents: the discount is cents * percent /
100, rounded half up as (cents * percent + 50) / 100. Doing it in
double (cents * 0.15) works until it doesn't — 0.15 is not exactly
representable, and some prices round the wrong way.
AmountOff clamps with Math.max(0, ...): a 5.00 voucher on a 3.00 item
makes it free, not -2.00.
best is a min-by over apply: a loop keeping the best so far (strict <
keeps the first on a tie) or stream().min(comparingLong(d ->
d.apply(cents))). An empty list returning NoDiscount is the "null
object" pattern — the caller never has to check for null.

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/06.instructions:
**Concepts:** builder pattern · fluent API · validation · List.copyOf  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A quiz engine's Question has text, options, the index of the right
option and a point value. Finish the nested Builder: each setter
returns the builder so calls chain; option(...) adds one option;
points default to 1. build() checks everything at once and throws
IllegalStateException for: blank text, fewer than 2 options, an answer
index that is not one of the options, or points below 1. The built
Question's option list can never change.

    Question.builder().text("2 + 2?").option("3").option("4")
        .answer(1).build()                  → points 1, options [3, 4]
    ...with one option only                  → IllegalStateException

hint: "return this;" is what makes a setter chainable.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/06.explanation:
A record with five components and a constructor full of positional
arguments is unreadable at the call site — new Question("2+2?",
List.of("3","4"), 1, 1): which 1 is which? A builder names each part,
lets optional parts default, and gathers validation in ONE place:
build().
Each setter stores its value and returns this, so calls chain. The
builder is mutable on purpose; the thing it builds is not.
Why validate in build() and not in each setter? Because some rules
involve several fields (the answer index depends on how many options
there are), and options arrive one call at a time. IllegalStateException
fits: no argument was bad on its own, the builder is in a state that
cannot produce a valid Question.
The built Question copies the options with List.copyOf — an
unmodifiable snapshot. Without the copy, a caller who keeps using the
builder (adding another option) would change an already-built
question behind its back. (Records' compact constructors are a good
place for that copy, so even code that bypasses the builder is safe.)

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/07.instructions:
**Concepts:** sealed interfaces · records · instanceof patterns · immutability  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A to-do manager's commands form a CLOSED family: the sealed interface
Command permits exactly Add, Complete and Rename (records, above the
tests). Write apply: given the current tasks and a command, return the
NEW list of tasks (the input list is never changed). Add gets the next
id (highest id + 1; 1 for an empty list); Complete marks a task done;
Rename changes a title. Complete or Rename of an unknown id →
IllegalArgumentException. Then write describe, a one-line summary.

    apply([], new Add("milk"))     → [Task[id=1, title=milk, done=false]]
    apply(tasks, new Complete(1))        → task 1 now done
    describe(new Rename(2, "eggs"))      → "rename #2 to eggs"

hint: `if (c instanceof Add add)` tests, casts and names in one step.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/07.explanation:
A sealed interface lists its implementations: `sealed interface Command
permits Add, Complete, Rename`. Nobody else can implement it, so code
that handles those three handles every command — the type system now
knows the family is closed. Records make each command a one-line data
carrier.
Java 17 dispatches on such a family with instanceof patterns: `if (c
instanceof Add add) { ... add.title() ... }`. (Java 21 adds pattern
`switch` with exhaustiveness checking — `case Add a ->` — which is the
real payoff of sealed types; on 17 the final `throw` after the if-chain
is the "can't happen" arm.)
The tasks are immutable records, so "completing" a task means building
a replacement — a small wither helps — and the list is rebuilt with
stream().map(...), replacing the one matching id. Returning a new list
leaves the caller's list untouched, which is what makes undo, history
and testing trivial.
Unknown ids: check that some task matched (anyMatch first, or count
replacements) and throw IllegalArgumentException — silently ignoring a
command for a task that does not exist hides bugs in the caller.
The next id is max(id) + 1, with 0 as the max of nothing: mapToInt(
Task::id).max().orElse(0) + 1. Using size() + 1 breaks the moment a
task is ever deleted.

javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/08.instructions:
**Concepts:** immutability · defensive copies · unmodifiable lists · withers  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

An order management tool passes Orders between components, so an Order
must be truly immutable. Finish the nested final class Order: the
constructor refuses an empty list and any line with quantity below 1
(IllegalArgumentException) and keeps its OWN copy of the lines; lines()
can't be used to change the order; withLine returns a new Order with
one more line and leaves this one alone; total is the sum of quantity
times unit price, in cents.

    var lines = new ArrayList<>(List.of(new Line("TEA", 2, 450)));
    var order = new Order(lines);
    lines.add(new Line("CAKE", 1, 300));     order.lines().size() → 1
    order.withLine(new Line("CAKE", 1, 300)).total()             → 1200

hint: final fields stop reassignment, not mutation of what they point to.
javabootcamp/05-classes-records-enums/08.explanation:
`private final List<Line> lines` does not make an Order immutable. final
only means the FIELD can't be reassigned; the list it points at can
still change. There are two leaks to plug.
Leak 1, in: if the constructor stores the caller's list, the caller
still holds a reference and can add lines afterwards. Copy on the way
in: List.copyOf(lines) makes an unmodifiable snapshot (and throws on
null elements, a bonus check).
Leak 2, out: if lines() returns the internal list and it is mutable,
any reader can change the order. Because the field already holds an
unmodifiable copy, returning it directly is safe — that is the second
payoff of copying with List.copyOf rather than new ArrayList<>().
Validate the COPY, not the original: validating the caller's list and
then copying leaves a gap where another thread could change it in
between (time-of-check to time-of-use).
"Changing" an immutable object means building a new one: withLine
copies the current lines, adds one, and calls the constructor — which
re-validates. The old Order is untouched, so anyone holding it (a
receipt, an audit log) still sees what they were given.
Line is a record of immutable values, so sharing Line instances between
orders is safe; a mutable element type would need copying too.
